data.text: Two. Coca-Cola in Iran

data.caption: Coca-Cola factory in Mashhad

data.text: Carbonated drinks entered Iran around the 1950s-60s (the 1330s-1340s in the Iranian calendar) and grew more popular by the day. Like many countries, the players in this new market — from the moment of its formation — were two American names: Coca-Cola and Pepsi. Each of these two brands was produced in one or more Iranian factories. From then to today these two names have been part of the story of soft drinks in Iran. (Jam-e Jam) But this presence has had many controversies, especially after the Islamic Revolution of 1979. Two main reasons can be found for these controversies: first the American-ness of these companies, and second the perennial rumours about their connections and support. With Pepsi, controversy began with the rumour of the brand's link to the Bahá'í faith in the 1960s — to the point that it even reached a fatwa from Imam Khomeini against buying and selling Pepsi. (Hawzah News)

Rumours about these companies are not exclusive to Iran. Coca-Cola's official international site has created a dedicated page titled "Rumours and misinformation" that responds to six common claims about the company and its products. Of these six questions, two concern the company's relationship with the Israeli regime.

data.caption: The rumours and misinformation page on Coca-Cola's official site

data.text: Khoshgovar, Nooshab, Coca-Cola

One of the plants that produced Coca-Cola in Iran before the Islamic Revolution was Khoshgovar Mashhad. Khoshgovar's cooperation with Coca-Cola continued for several years after the Revolution, until it was finally halted at the beginning of the 1980s.

During the war with Iraq, American sanctions on Iran were strongly enforced. Pepsi and Coca-Cola producers — including Khoshgovar — who had lost access to those companies' concentrate had to switch to Iranian beverage syrups and continue production with them. But with the start of the 1990s (1370s) and shifts in the Iran-US relationship — and the loosening of the sanctions regime on the other hand — domestic bottlers were once again tempted to cooperate with the American giants. (Jam-e Jam) (CNN)

data.caption: Coca-Cola production line in Iran

data.text: Khoshgovar managed in 1991 (1370) to re-establish its relationship with Coca-Cola and resume production under licence. But this time a new player had also saddled its horse to powerfully enter the market: a new company called Nooshab. In 1993 (1372) Nooshab signed a contract with Coca-Cola in which the American company committed to investing $15 million and acquiring 27% of the company's shares, participating directly in beverage production in Iran. This was the first investment by a foreign company in Iran after the Revolution — and it came from an American company in the beverage industry!

But in this new competition things did not go as Nooshab — the newcomer — had hoped. In 1994 (1373), just a year after the Nooshab-Coca-Cola contract, then-US president Bill Clinton intensified anti-Iran sanctions. Coca-Cola, which had only paid half its share of the partnership, refused to pay the rest. Nooshab, which had just started production and had prepared around 40 million glass bottles bearing the Coca-Cola brand, was suddenly even cut off from receiving Coca-Cola concentrate.

data.caption: A Coca-Cola bottle attributed to Nooshab

data.text: After Nooshab's follow-ups with Coca-Cola produced no result, the company sued its American partner and won the case. Nooshab also decided to fill the Coca-Cola bottles it was stuck with using Iranian beverage syrup and put them on the market. With this action Nooshab found itself sued in return by Coca-Cola, the trademark owner — Coca-Cola took its counter-claim to Iranian court, demanding damages for trademark infringement. The complaint succeeded and resulted in Nooshab paying $5 million in damages to the American company. (Jam-e Jam) (CNN) (BBC) This case clearly shows that, contrary to many people's common assumption, using a registered, internationally recognised brand without the owner's permission can carry heavy consequences for the offender.
The 22-day war and the Coca-Cola controversies

Let's go back a little. At the time of the Nooshab-Coca-Cola legal dispute, the Iranian beverage market briefly saw both the original Khoshgovar Coca-Cola and the unofficial Nooshab Coca-Cola side by side. But Nooshab, given its problems, gradually faded and was finally bought by Khoshgovar in 2013 (1392). Khoshgovar thus became the sole flag-bearer of Coca-Cola in Iran. (Khoshgovar's HiDay brand website) (CNN)

But the Americanness of Coca-Cola and the rumours about its relationship with and support for the Israeli regime have always created sensitivities about it and its producer Khoshgovar. The issue becomes especially hot — and on everyone's lips — when the Israeli regime's aggressions and conflicts escalate. One such moment was the second half of the 2000s (1380s) during the regime's attacks on Gaza. These attacks prompted revolutionary segments and certain officials to push back against Coca-Cola's presence in the Iranian market.

One of the pioneers on this issue was the Mashhad People's Demand Forum, which in an open letter to Khoshgovar's directors asked them to explain the relationship with the Coca-Cola company. (Source) This came especially after the publication of interviews with international Coca-Cola executives confirming the company's presence in the Iranian market. (Reuters news agency) This letter and similar events again brought Coca-Cola and Israel-supporting companies into Iranian media headlines. At that time Manouchehr Mottaki, the then-foreign-minister, announced the handover of seven volumes of brochures listing the names of Zionist or multinational companies in which Israelis held shares. He noted an important point in explaining it: "Multinational companies have created a kind of intermingling that makes them hard to identify." (Asr-e Iran) Something that seems to be true for Coca-Cola too.

In 2008 (1387) parliament passed a new law called the "Law obliging the government to comprehensively support the oppressed people of Palestine". Among its clauses was a ban on the government importing goods from — and contracting with — companies whose main shareholders were Zionist entities. (Parliament website) Just days after this resolution, Mehrabian, the then-industry-minister, ordered the suspension of all companies in which Zionists held part of the ownership abroad. (ISNA news agency) He then gave Khoshgovar a deadline to clarify its relationship with Coca-Cola. (Asr-e Iran) This may have indicated that Zionist shareholding in Coca-Cola was already taken for granted by the Industry Ministry — and that the only thing to clarify was whether this company was linked to Khoshgovar.

The strange thing was that Khoshgovar always printed on its product — produced with the Industry Ministry's own permits — the phrase "Filled under licence from the Coca-Cola Company". So by the rules, this ministry must have endorsed that claim. Yet the minister assumed the claim untrue and sought a confession from Khoshgovar!

data.caption: "Filled under licence from the Coca-Cola Company" printed on Khoshgovar's beverages

data.text: Khoshgovar reacted quickly to the minister's inquiry and in a statement denied any link with American Coca-Cola or any payment to it. To dispel suspicions, the company invoked the keyword "Ireland". One Khoshgovar director said in an interview: "We have always purchased our needed essence from Ireland and have not had — and will not have — any relationship with the Coca-Cola Company or the United States […] and have not paid any sums to Coca-Cola for any reason." (ISNA) (Fars) A strange response that was hoped would somewhat calm public and even government concerns.

Even so, the issue remained unclear and many questions surrounded it. Even Ayatollah Alamolhoda, the Friday-prayer leader of Mashhad, was asked about it. He replied that he had known this factory's investors for fifty years and knew them to be religiously devout and Iranian! But the Coca-Cola issue, he said, is complicated, and after meeting with the company's officials and the ministry's representative he still couldn't reach a conclusion about whether the factory's product was Zionist or not. (Mashregh)

The matter of publishing the lists also remained a recurring feature of those years' news. Lists that the Foreign Ministry was legally required to compile of Zionist companies — but, despite media noise, were never reliably published. From Manouchehr Mottaki's seven brochures and Hassan Qashqavi's letter to the National Security Commission, to the claim by Khandouzi, the 13th government's finance minister, that lists were declared to the Trade Promotion Organisation — and then Speaker Ghalibaf's request a few days later for the list to be released to prevent imports. (Jahan News) (Student news agency) (Hamshahri) These responses showed the issue is more complicated than the government wants — or is able — to resolve.
Al-Aqsa Storm and intensifying controversies

Throughout these years the tug-of-war over Khoshgovar, Coca-Cola, Israel and their relationships never ended. But the Israeli regime's new assault on Gaza after Al-Aqsa Storm (7 October 2023) again lit the fuse on the Khoshgovar-Coca-Cola affair. One of the events that drew much media attention was a live-TV clash between presenters Seyed Hossein Hosseini and Elmira Sharifi Moghaddam about Coca-Cola and Pepsi. (Video of the on-air clash about Coca-Cola)

Parliament representatives gradually entered the conversation too — including Ali Khezrian, spokesperson for the Article-90 commission, who said: "If the link of products like Coca-Cola and Nestlé with the parent companies is established, we must boycott them." (Nour News) That is — nearly two decades after this question was first publicly raised, the government had still not been able to confirm or deny this link! Although earlier, Asefari, then-deputy economic-foreign-minister, had said: "Coca-Cola producers inside the country told us in meetings that they have no relationship with the Coca-Cola Company". (Shargh)

As the regime's crimes in Gaza widened, media efforts to solve this old puzzle also intensified. But Khoshgovar's executives, having grown used over many years to these questions, unverified claims and empty threats, did not even feel any need to respond to the media. For example, Tebyan media published the account of its follow-up with Khoshgovar and the dismissive answers from company officials. (Tebyan) Mashhad's Sobh-e Toos news outlet, having approached one of Khoshgovar's directors on the issue, was told: "You won't get anywhere — don't bother pursuing this matter!" (Sobh-e Toos)

But in October 2024 (Mehr 1403) a strange piece of news suddenly emerged: "Coca-Cola production in Iran halted". It was claimed that, due to the US administration's positions and new sanctions, Coca-Cola had cut its cooperation with Iranian companies, and we would soon see the end of Coca-Cola drinks in the Iranian market. The interesting point was that none of the many outlets and newspapers publishing this story cited a credible source, attributing it instead to "news circulated on social media"! (Eqtesad News) (Etemad) Even so, an accompanying analytical current rode on this wave and lamented the supposed event. These analyses made tragic comparisons between Coca-Cola's exit and the importation of iPhones, cars and home appliances, explaining the role of mafias and rivals in this event and its tragic consequences for the people and the Iranian beverage market. (Ettelaat)

Nothing happened to Coca-Cola products in the market after this news, and the drinks remained as abundant in shop fridges as before. But this news once again raised many questions in the Iranian consumer's mind: was Coca-Cola in Iran in the first place, that it could now intend to leave?! Hadn't Khoshgovar's officials said we never had any relationship with American Coca-Cola? What, in the end, is the reality of Coca-Cola in Iran?!
Coca-Cola is in Iran. Full stop.

The reality is that the Khoshgovar-Coca-Cola relationship has never been mysterious or hidden. But owing to the disorder of the public and media space and unfamiliarity with basic business principles, it has been possible — through projection, ambiguity, doubt and misinformation — for this matter to look like a complicated, unanswered question for years. Let us review all the evidence of this relationship together:
Evidence 1 — Coca-Cola's own admission

Khoshgovar is an official bottler in the Coca-Cola system, holding the right to produce and exclusively distribute inside Iran's geographical borders — exactly like the 200 or so other official bottlers around the world in this system, responsible for producing and getting Coca-Cola products to consumers. Khoshgovar is also listed on Coca-Cola's global official website as one of the company's bottling partners for the Eurasia & Middle East region. (Coca-Cola website)

data.caption: Khoshgovar's name among Coca-Cola's official partners on the company's official website

data.text: Evidence 2 — Under Coca-Cola licence

Throughout the years Coca-Cola products have been on the Iranian market, the front has always carried "Original" and the back "Under licence from International Coca-Cola". Contrary to common assumption, printing such phrases on a product that is officially produced and distributed under legal permits carries serious legal weight and must be approved by legal authorities. This shows that Khoshgovar itself has tried to convince its customers that they are dealing with an original Coca-Cola.
Evidence 3 — Trademark

The Coca-Cola product produced and distributed by Khoshgovar legally and officially uses the name, logo, visual identity, bottle and other trademarks belonging to the International Coca-Cola Company — assets that are also registered and officially protected in Iran. (Document Registration 1) (Document Registration 2) Contrary to common belief, Iran has proper laws for the protection of trademarks (brands). Under Article 31 of the Patent, Industrial Designs and Trademarks Law, "the exclusive right to use a mark belongs to whoever has registered it in accordance with this law". According to this law "the use of any mark registered in Iran, by anyone other than the owner of the mark, is subject to the owner's agreement." So Khoshgovar has naturally been able to use Coca-Cola's marks under some kind of agreement with the company:

Per Article 40 of the Patent, Industrial Designs and Trademarks Law: "The owner of a registered mark may file suit in court against any person who uses the mark without its consent, or against any person committing an act that would ordinarily lead to violation of the rights arising from the registration of the mark. These rights cover use of a mark that is similar to the registered mark and whose use for similar goods or services causes confusion to the public." The earlier case of Coca-Cola's lawsuit against Nooshab for using the brand without an agreement — which an Iranian court ruled in favour of the brand owner — was mentioned above. This case clearly demonstrates the strength of the country's laws in protecting companies' commercial assets.

data.caption: Commercial assets registered under the name "The Coca-Cola Company" in Iran's Document Registration Organisation

data.text: Evidence 4 — Competitors' silence

Using another company's brand without permission is clearly an anti-competitive act and an instance of unfair competition under the law (Chapter Six of the Industrial Property Protection Law). (Parliament website) That is, the law does not allow one company — while competitors have to spend a significant portion of their resources on marketing and advertising — to officially use another company's brand without cost. A brand whose owner spends billions of dollars a year on advertising and reinforcement. If Khoshgovar's use of the Coca-Cola brand were done without Coca-Cola's permission, Khoshgovar's competitors could have easily sued the company under existing laws. They could also have used the same brand on their own products and easily expanded their market share. As it is, Khoshgovar — by its own director's admission — has been able to grow its market share through this very brand: "Our sales market depends on this name and we cannot remove it." (Aftab News)

Yet over all these years, none of Khoshgovar's competitors has taken either of these two steps, and Coca-Cola production has remained exclusively with Khoshgovar. We can therefore conclude that Khoshgovar's use of the Coca-Cola brand is definitely with the brand owner's official permission.
Three. The Coca-Cola - Khoshgovar contract

The information, documents and reasoning presented so far adequately establish Khoshgovar's direct relationship with Coca-Cola — but from July 2024 (Tir 1403) onwards, they are barely needed any more! On that date, a letter was published with a very important attachment — an attachment that effectively cleared away any ambiguity and doubt raised about Coca-Cola in Iran over all those years:
War in Ukraine, confession in Iran!

data.caption: The Trade Development Organisation's instruction asking that the export of all beverages produced by Khoshgovar under Coca-Cola licence be prevented.

data.text: It started when, with the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war, Coca-Cola in March 2022 (Esfand 1400) officially announced it would suspend its activity and product sales in Russia. This sudden decision gradually — as warehouse stocks ran down — built up pent-up demand for the company's products in the Russian market. At that time some traders seized the opportunity and bought Khoshgovar-produced Coca-Cola drinks in Iran for export to Russia.

data.caption: A Khoshgovar-made Coca-Cola can in Russia

data.text: As the issue grew, in July 2024 (Tir 1403) the Trade Development Organisation, in a letter, asked customs to prevent the export of beverages produced by Khoshgovar. (National laws and regulations database) This was actually a request that Khoshgovar itself had sent to the Trade Development Organisation, and the reason was nothing other than the terms of its official contract with the American Coca-Cola company — under which Khoshgovar was only permitted to sell Coca-Cola's products within the territorial borders of the Islamic Republic of Iran. This letter had a very important attachment too: the text of the official contract signed between Khoshgovar Tehran Joint-Stock Company, Iran and The Coca-Cola Atlanta Company, USA.
Read the text of the Coca-Cola - Khoshgovar contract on the National laws and regulations database.
A contract which, before anything else, called to mind the statements and claims made by Khoshgovar and its directors:
"…we have not had — and will not have — any relationship with the Coca-Cola Company or the United States at any time…"
data.caption: Mehdi Sayyadian — board member of Khoshgovar Tehran — 19 January 2009 (29 Dey 1387) (Source: IRNA)

data.text: Below we examine and analyse the important and interesting clauses of this contract. Some of these can resolve common doubts about the official presence of international companies in Iran — especially Coca-Cola:
Articles 1 and 28 — From Atlanta to Tehran

As explained earlier, Khoshgovar is part of Coca-Cola's international bottling, distribution and sales system whose ultimate goal is to increase Coca-Cola's sales and revenue while generating revenue for its partners. For this reason, Article 28 specifies and emphasises Coca-Cola's rights over this system. In the Coca-Cola system, the right and exclusivity to produce, distribute and sell the product in each defined geographical area is granted to one or more bottlers. Similarly, under Article 1, Khoshgovar holds exclusivity to supply Coca-Cola only within the geographical borders of the Islamic Republic of Iran.
Article 13 — Guarantee of benefits

One might naively claim that although Coca-Cola has given Khoshgovar the right to use the brand, this does not mean the company is gaining any benefit. But Article 13 explicitly states that all rights and benefits arising from use of the trademarks and other elements must guarantee the company's benefits — at the top of which is increased sales and brand penetration of the Coca-Cola Company.
Preamble (d) — Irish supplier!

Clause (d) of the contract's preamble can clarify the role of "Ireland" that had cast a shadow over Khoshgovar's relationship with American Coca-Cola — a country whose mention created ambiguity among media, the public and even officials who lacked deep familiarity with the issue. This clause specifies that, in supplying concentrate to Khoshgovar, the Coca-Cola company has designated a number of third-party companies as "authorised suppliers".

In addition to America, Coca-Cola has factories producing concentrate in some other parts of the world. Among these are concentrate-making plants in Costa Rica, India and Brazil, all of which were set up in recent years with Coca-Cola investment and are wholly owned by it. (Costa Rica Star) (Times of India) (Reuters)

In the Coca-Cola system, four main geographical regions are defined: North America, South America, Europe-Middle East-Africa and Asia — and each of the companies mentioned, depending on its capacity, supplies part of the needs of bottlers in these regions. (Investopedia) Among the most important regions where Coca-Cola produces its concentrates is Ireland. One of these Irish concentrate-making plants was in Drogheda, which actually halted activity in 2008 (1387). In the mid-2000s and following the Mashhad people's-demand forum's follow-ups, several Iranian and foreign outlets named Ireland and the Drogheda concentrate plant as Khoshgovar's supplier. When Drogheda was asked about this alleged relationship with Khoshgovar, the company referred the matter to Coca-Cola. A Coca-Cola executive was then questioned. He confirmed concentrate sales to Iran but again stayed silent on the source. (Mehr) (The Times) (CNN)

Some time later, Khoshgovar executives effectively confirmed Ireland as the concentrate supply origin. (ISNA) Coca-Cola had several concentrate-producing factories in Ireland — though in recent years it closed most of them, including Drogheda, and consolidated their capacity in the Ballina plant. (Irish Times) (Eurofound) Given the history of supplying Khoshgovar from Ireland, one can guess that the "authorised supplier" for buying concentrate mentioned in Khoshgovar's contract with Coca-Cola is this very Ballina factory. Even so, the matter is of little importance — because as the documents cited show, all the concentrate-producing factories in the Coca-Cola system, anywhere in the world, are under that company's ownership. This is especially important for Coca-Cola to keep the formula confidential. So whichever concentrate plant Khoshgovar buys its raw materials from, this purchase is ultimately made directly from the Coca-Cola company, and the resulting revenue belongs to American Coca-Cola.
Article 23 — Price-conditioned

This part of the contract confirms the explanations above. Under this clause, the price of the concentrate purchased by Khoshgovar is also set by the Coca-Cola company. So it's clear that the concentrate seller is effectively Coca-Cola. Under the contract, even the cap on the final product (beverage) sale price in the Iranian market is set by Coca-Cola.
Article 25 — Sanctioned without damages

One of the points often invoked to deny the official presence of foreign companies and their products in Iran is the issue of monetary and banking sanctions and the impossibility of moving money to and from Iran. The present contract, signed between an Iranian and an American company, clearly shows that monetary transfers between them happen without problems. Because, first, in clause (a) of Article 23, the Coca-Cola company's right to determine "shipping and payment conditions and the acceptable currency or currencies" is mentioned.

Second, clause (a) of Article 25 stipulates that if "the company, the authorised suppliers or the bottler cannot obtain the foreign currency that must be paid abroad for importing concentrate or…", "the company or the bottler may terminate this contract immediately, without liability for damages, …". So if there were a serious problem moving money, including such a clause in the contract would be meaningless, or under it the contract would already easily have been terminated by one of the parties.
Article 31 — Quarantine!

One of the more interesting parts of the Coca-Cola - Khoshgovar contract is Article 31. This article assures that if, due to actions by the public or the government, either party cannot fulfil its obligations, no responsibility will fall on them. Among these actions it explicitly mentions: "being placed on a blacklist, boycotted, sanctioned by an independent nation or a supranational body of independent nations occurring in any manner; or … being designated as an enemy of a nation; a legal ruling or administrative action (including the revocation of any government permit …); a public boycott; quarantine; …" The explicit, clear listing of such items in a contract is — though striking — a sign of Coca-Cola's and Khoshgovar's awareness, and concern, about the threats they face in Iran and across the world from people, governments and movements like BDS.
Four. Famous claims about Coca-Cola
A humanitarian exemption! Coca-Cola and US sanctions

With Coca-Cola's official presence in Iran clarified, an important question comes to mind: isn't Iran under the harshest sanctions? Then how does an American company officially operate in Iran without any problem? The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) also asked Coca-Cola this question in a letter, demanding an explanation. In its official response, Coca-Cola — while confirming presence and activity in Iran through licensing a local bottler — said the activity is under a licence obtained from the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). (SEC) The company's communications director, in a letter responding to an article published in the Irish Times, also pointed to the OFAC licence and explained that the concentrate sold to Iran is classified as food and is therefore covered by sanctions exemptions. He emphasised that Coca-Cola's relationship with Iran is not a sanctions evasion but is being conducted through a legal loophole. (Irish Times)

The New York Times has published a list of companies that have obtained OFAC licences for commercial activity with Iran under the US Congress's humanitarian(!) exemptions — and Coca-Cola is on it. (New York Times) Note that in some areas — medicine, food, agriculture, education and so on — the US government has granted licences for American companies and institutions to operate in Iran. (Wall Street Journal)
Real Coke is different! Examining a popular claim

One of the recurring statements about Coca-Cola — used to deny the presence of the company's real products in Iran — is that if you've tried real Coke outside Iran you'll notice its flavour is very different and better than the similar drink available in Iran. But this claim is not exclusive to Iran. One of the frequently asked questions answered on Coca-Cola's official international site is this very flavour difference of Coca-Cola in different countries. Coca-Cola has rejected this claim and explains this impression as a result of factors like consumption temperature and storage conditions. (Coca-Cola website) In any case, what is certain is that even if the flavour difference is real, it does not mean the product is not genuine — because this matter covers the entire Coca-Cola system, prompting the company to respond to it.

data.text: Five. From fizzy to pulpy: Coca-Cola's brand portfolio in Iran

Although not all Coca-Cola brands are present in Iran, the company's brand portfolio in Iran is still varied. The main brand Coca-Cola and its sub-brands (Zero and Light), Fanta and Fanta Light, Sprite and Sprite Light — all carbonated drinks — alongside the bottled water Dasani are the Coca-Cola company's primary, direct brands produced in Iran. (Coca-Cola website)

Another important brand produced in Iran under Coca-Cola licence is Canada Dry. Canada Dry is an old brand with Canadian origins. The brand, which over its lifetime has passed between several companies, currently belongs to the Keurig Dr Pepper group. (Keurig Dr Pepper) But in the business world, companies sometimes use other companies' capacity to access markets they themselves cannot. Keurig Dr Pepper, in regions where it cannot operate directly, has granted Coca-Cola the rights to some of its brands — including Canada Dry. For example, in the Japanese market Coca-Cola holds the rights to distribute Canada Dry. (Coca-Cola website)

In Iran the Canada Dry brand has long been known by the public as "the yellow soda". So Khoshgovar, in the late 2000s (1380s), decided to use this familiarity and — given its relationship with Coca-Cola — revive its position in the Iranian market. (Khabar Online)

data.text: Canada Dry is registered in Iran by European Refreshments — an Irish company belonging to Coca-Cola. (Document Registration) (Coca-Cola EP) (Bloomberg) It is therefore clear that this brand is owned in Iran by Coca-Cola, and Khoshgovar has been able to supply it in Iran on the same basis. Coca-Cola's 2006 letter to the SEC also stated that after supplying the Coca-Cola, Fanta and Sprite brands, the company was seeking permission from OFAC to supply some other brands — including Canada Dry — in Iran. Something that came to pass two years later. (SEC) In addition, the Minute Maid juice, Powerade sports-drink and Costa Coffee brands — all owned by Coca-Cola — have at various points been present in the Iranian market through local production, import or smuggling. (Coca-Cola website)

data.text: Alongside Coca-Cola-owned brands, other brands are also present in Iran which — through Coca-Cola's investments and partnerships with their owners — fall under the company's umbrella. The most important of these are the Rani fruit drinks and Barbican malt beverages. In 2005 (1384) Saudi Arabia's Aujan group entered the Iranian market by founding Aujan Iranian (East Trade Industries) and supplying Rani fruit drinks. (Rasmio) A few years later this company invested to produce Rani products and Barbican malt drinks domestically — operations that continue extensively to this day. (IRNA) (Ettelaat)

In 2011 (1390) Coca-Cola made a $980 million investment in Aujan group's beverages business. Following this investment, two companies — Rani Refreshments and Aujan-Coca-Cola Beverages — were born. In this important partnership Coca-Cola took 50% and 49% of these two companies' shares respectively. (Coca-Cola Company) Rani Refreshments owns and maintains the Rani and Barbican brands, while Aujan-Coca-Cola handles production and distribution. (Aujan 1) (Aujan 2) Under the same arrangement, the Rani and Barbican brands are registered in Iran by Rani Refreshments — making them identifiable as Coca-Cola-company brands. (Document Registration 1) (Document Registration 2)

Iranian consumers may also encounter some of Coca-Cola's special brands outside Iran. For example, the drink Crystal is widely available in Iraq. This brand also belongs to the Coca-Cola family of brands and is produced by Turkey's CCİ (İçecek) bottler. CCİ is one of the larger bottlers in the Coca-Cola system, holding the rights to distribute the company's brands in many central- and west-Asian countries including Iraq. Coca-Cola itself now also owns 20% of CCİ. (CCİ 1) (CCİ 2)

data.text: Finally: Coca-Cola and supporting Israel

The tangled story of Coca-Cola's presence in Iran has, after years, finally found its loose end today. A thread which, once pulled, perhaps answers half the consumer's questions. Yes — Coca-Cola is in Iran. But the other half — the accusations against Coca-Cola regarding its relationship with Israel — remains unanswered. That half will be revealed soon in the second part of qlist's Coca-Cola dossier.
